sahne: A figure approaches the gate with faltering steps. From the felt sack on his back rises the scent of roasted millet and charred soot; his left hand fiercely clutches a leather pouch to his chest as though guarding his very life.
sorular: You claim you fled the plain trampled by Mongol steeds, farmer; if the beylik fields burned, which mountain gorge did you cross to reach this pass?

I broke away from the plain of Erzincan, effendi... At harvest time black smoke choked the sky; hoofbeats tore through the crops. Grain turned to ashes, the village scattered. I shut my eyes and fled hither.
Cease your lies! You were present when the Bey's granary was torched; does this seed belong to that looted store?

S-seed, did you say, effendi? No... The bey spurred his mount and barred himself inside the citadel, abandoning the folk to the fire. I did not steal this seed from the granary... It was the final ear of my own plot! The stench of naphtha clung to me from the plain, by heaven I am no thief!
If you are no thief, why do you stammer? Do you know the fate of the shepherd who fell to wolves on the ridge last night?

I know, effendi... The ox-herder you turned away from the gate yesterday was torn apart on the rocks; I heard the howling from the creek! Do not cast me to the wolves as well... Take the purse, take the millet, spare my life!
zahire_hirsizi_suphesi
Your land burned, your heart burned... Are you hungry; do you desire water?

Blessings upon you, guard effendi... For three days nothing has passed my throat save muddy water from the creek. I would accept a dry crust, if only this seed does not perish. Grant me a furrow of earth, and next summer your granary shall brim full.
If you entrust this seed to our village soil, we shall grant you hearth and bowl.

The earth does not hold grudges, effendi; so long as man is not ungrateful, the ear of grain bows in bounty. I will pour my sweat into your soil; with the first harvest, your orphans shall eat their fill.
If the Bey's granary burned, every single grain in that sack is worth gold. What will you contribute to the settlement?

The pouch looks small, yet within it sleep a thousand ears of wheat. Give me a hut against the palisade; half the seed goes to your village store, the rest I plant in your plot. Before winter ends it will sprout green.
At the threshold you said 'I will let no man tread upon this seed'; a man does not risk his neck for a fistful of common millet. In that leather pouch, do you conceal some precious gem of the court?

I guard the light of my eyes, effendi. Pure yellow kunduru seed wheat... It is but a fistful, yet it holds the blessing of three valleys in its heart. I pressed it to my chest so no greedy eye might covet it.
If drought strikes or spring rains fail, will this seed save the village?
I am a man who coaxed rye from cracked stones in dry creek beds, guard. Earth requires patience; I will dig trenches from the brook and clear the pebbles. One handful of this seed yields sevenfold.
The seal of the Bey has been ripped from the neck of that pouch; if bailiffs track it, they will torch our village too!
There is no seal, effendi... It was torn away! The sanjak bey fled long ago; Mongol horsemen tore through the valley. If we do not establish order here, none of us will survive the winter!
muhur_tahrif_suphesi
You bow humbly at the gate, but how do I know you will not disrupt village peace tomorrow?
Were I one of the rebellious sort, I would have taken to the crags with the brigands, effendi. I earn my bread from stone; a pallet in the hayloft at evening prayer is all I ask.
Did you encounter the refugees we turned away yesterday on the mountain trail?

I saw them, effendi... They huddled behind the boulders. One muttered, 'The heart of the guard at the gate is carved of flint.' I did not say so; I said, 'He is a man of justice; he knows the worth of seed.' Do not prove me wrong.

yanitlar.ret: Do not cast me back into the frozen dark, guard... The wolves will pick my bones before dawn. Have mercy!
yanitlar.kabul: May heaven bless your threshold! You will see; you will not regret granting me shelter.
yanitlar.rusvet: Take this purse... Let it stay between the two of us. Just lift the latch and let me slip inside.

not: Reject first. After one reply, Accept and Bribe unlock. No Barracks.
acilis: Peace be upon you, guard effendi... For days I have crossed mountain and stone. Behind me lies an ash-gray plain trampled by Mongol horses. In my hands I hold only this fistful of seed and a sack of millet. I will let no man tread upon this seed; I shall bury it into the earth.

sahne: A man in a dust-whitened kaftan pauses to catch his breath at the gate threshold. Tucked beneath his arm is a tightly rolled bolt of purple wool broadcloth, untouched by mire; faint metallic clinking echoes between its folds.
sorular: You say the Kayseri bazaar turned to ash; with looters burning the Hunat Hatun arcade, how did you pull that single bolt of Frankish broadcloth from the flames?

The caravan was raided, master! The camel-driver fled and the apprentices scattered. In fear for my life, I clutched the finest wool broadcloth from the loom right out of the blaze. Forty years of labor rests beneath my arm.
What did you hide inside the cloth? Your fingers prod at coins inside rather than the fabric!

N-not coins, master... That is, the brass key of the loom and the scale dirhem weights are wrapped inside! Though I have no face left to return to the bazaar, I still keep the honor of my craft... And if I hold forty dirhems of silver, it is my own lawful earning!
Are you from Master Karaca's Ahi hearth? Fraudulent cloth shall never enter this village!

Is Master Karaca in this village? Mercy, master, he is our guild elder! May my hearth be ruined if I bring unlawful cloth onto the soil he treads! Let him inspect the bolt himself; if a single thread proves rotten, strike off my head!
gizli_akce_suphesi
You say your loom went up in smoke; did the Ahi warden in the covered market not protect the merchants, and who started the fire?
Our Ahi warden chained the gate, but brigands poured naphtha from the roof, master. Before the beylik cavalry could arrive, the bazaar was ash. Whoever saved his skin fled to the mountains.
You could not save your apprentice, yet here you can train new apprentices.

May God be pleased with you... Grant me a corner beneath an awning; I will teach the village orphans to weave broadcloth and sew felt cloaks, so long as my hands stay busy and those flames leave my mind.
Your glossy broadcloth does not suit our village's coarse felt; lords wear such cloth. What bribe do you offer?

Let me cut three cubits of this fine purple broadcloth for you, master guard. Have a braided tunic sewn and walk like a sanjak bey on feast days. I will leave two silver pieces from the shop's brass weights beside it—just close your eyes and let me pass.
This village needs no draper; villagers wear coarse felt. What use are you here?

Coarse felt needs a cutter too, gatekeeper! I do not weave broadcloth for lords alone; I reinforce shepherd felt, patch soldiers' saddlebags, and stitch tent canvas. An idle hand slips into sin, and my hand never rests.
The soldiers' barracks tents leak rain; can you reinforce them?
I will sew a double stitch with tarred cord, master! Then rub beeswax over the seams; even if stones rain from the sky, not a drop will seep through. Just provide me coarse needles and beeswax.
Yesterday we refused entry to a saddler fleeing the Kayseri caravan; did you hear of him?

I heard, master... I saw him by the roadside fountain weeping that the guard was stern and shut the gate in his face. Yet that saddler was a lackey of the extortionists, I know him! My record in the Ahi ledger is spotless; I beg you, do not count me as his like.

yanitlar.rusvet: Let me cut three cubits from this fine purple broadcloth for you, master guard. Have a gold-braided tunic tailored and walk like a sanjak bey on feast days. Put these two silver dirhems in your pouch too, and look the other way as I pass.
yanitlar.kabul: May God be pleased with you! No later than tomorrow I shall set up my loom in the village square and spread the bounty of cloth here, and pay my respects to Master Karaca.
yanitlar.ret: If I am left out on this mountain with this cloth, brigands will slit my throat. Do not cast me to the wolves like the saddler you drove away yesterday—have mercy, guard.

not: Bribe first. After one reply, Accept and Reject unlock. No Barracks.
acilis: They called me the clothier of the Kayseri bazaar... Forty years of looms turned to smoke in a single night, and only this bolt of broadcloth remains. If I can find a loom and a quiet corner in your market, I shall earn my bread once more.

sahne: The straps on the limping trooper's breastplate are snapped. He leans on his broken lance like a staff, dried blood from his left temple matted into his beard; in his eyes linger both exhaustion and barracks fury.
sorular: When the army broke at Sivas, what did you shatter your lance against, and whom did you fight, trooper?

We fell into an ambush in the gorge, master. Cavalry cut off our vanguard; I drove my lance into a horse's chest, but its barding was iron and the shaft snapped clean in two. The mount trampled over me, and I rolled into a ditch and survived.
Are you a deserter who abandoned the standard? If an execution firman arrives, they will hang your head from the wall!

Watch your tongue, gatekeeper! I never abandoned the standard! While my corporal was crushed beneath the hooves, I stuffed the banner inside my tunic! For three days I crawled through mire! Had I fled, I would have fled to the palace, not the steppe! Step back a pace, or I will make a rampart of this broken lance!
Your wrath proves your valor, yet law is law; if you surrender to the barracks, your life will be spared.
My life is already pledged to the realm, master. Bring me before the castle warden; let me mark the cavalry ambush on the map, and then hang me or post me on the tower as you will!
firari_asker
The blood on your temple is matted in your beard, and your left leg trembles... You can barely stand.

As blood flows, sorrow lessens, master... Yet thirst has seared my lungs. For three days I drank from streams reeking of dead horses. Give me a bowl of well water, and I will gladly sleep like a hound at the barracks door.
There is clean bandage linen and vinegar in the infirmary; step inside and let us dress your wound.
May God be pleased with you, comrade... A soldier understands a soldier's plight. May my own sword coil around my neck if I ever forget this kindness.
Yesterday we turned away a trooper at the gate and he fell into the hands of brigands in the gorge. Did you see him?

I saw him, master... Brigands had surrounded him in the Karaboran gorge; he was begging them for food since the village refused him. I never bow to brigands! I would rather die of hunger than hold out my hand to the enemy; do not compare me to cowardly deserters!
Your leg limps and your wound is fresh. If we admit you to the barracks, will you not fall asleep on watch?

My wound will scab over, gatekeeper! My eyes are sharp and my ears are taut as a bowstring. Even with this broken lance I can stand lookout at the night crenel. I can scent an enemy's breath from a mile away.
What will you do if cavalry approaches by night?

With my left hand I will sound the horn, and with my right I will heave stones to the parapet. If horsemen prop ladders, I will bring boulders down upon their heads. Sleep easy, gatekeeper; I am no soldier who dozes on watch.
You said the Sultan is far away and order has collapsed, trooper; did the subashi at Sivas Castle abandon the standard, and who scattered the army?

The Sultan's army scattered and the beys turned on one another. The subashi in the citadel abandoned the banner to save his own skin, master. From now on these frontier villages must fend for themselves; no relief army is coming behind us.

yanitlar.kisla: May the barracks hearth smoke high! I will cast aside this broken shaft and draw a fresh spear from the rack. I will recount the enemy cavalry's tactics to the warden step by step; we shall hold this village firmer than a fortress.
yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, comrade... If I find a strip of linen and a bucket of water in the infirmary, I will bind my leg. Come morning, I will help deepen the trench around the village.
yanitlar.ret: Will you leave me out in tonight's frost covered in blood? Will you feed me to the wolves and crows like the soldier you turned away yesterday? May your mercy wither...

not: Barracks first. After one reply, Accept and Reject unlock. No Bribe.
acilis: My lance is broken, and my left leg is nearly spent. I have walked on foot all the way from the Sivas gorge. The Sultan is far away and order has collapsed... Grant me a bowl of hot soup and a corner to keep watch, and I will repay the rest with my blade.

sahne: A felt cloak rests on his shoulders, and behind him huddle two gaunt sheep. The wooden milk pail at his belt is empty, his fingers bruised purple from the cold; the breath of the beasts rises like steam in the frost.
sorular: You say Mongol riders burned the highland; when you loosed the flock onto the mountain and fled, why drag along these two skinny sheep—were they not a burden?

I had forty head of sheep, master guard... My shepherd hound gave its life as raidersringed the valley. I could not drive them all, yet these two are a breeding ram and ewe born on the snowy peaks, whose milk is healing. A village needs breeding stock like these.
The flanks of your sheep wheeze and foam clings to their nostrils; will you infect the village flock with pox or mange?

Do not slander me, master! This is no sheep-pox! For three days they starved among the crags and breathed smoke, that is why they wheeze! I will break the hand of anyone who harms my beasts! Give them a handful of dry straw, and within two days their foam will subside!
If contagion spreads, the whole village flock will perish; would that not be a pity for Yusuf's goats?

Did you say Yusuf? Is Yusuf, shepherd of Karabash, in this village? Ah, master, I know his goats well! Pen Akcha and Karaca in a separate fence and watch them for three days; if a single sore appears, I will slaughter the sheep with my own hands!
suru_hastaligi_riski
Your hands are bruised purple from the frost and your milk pail is cracked... Clearly these beasts are your companions in life.

Indeed they are, master guard... I took them into my arms the day they were born. Does a man part from his own child? Their mothers fell to wolves, and these remained to me. Put us in a corner of the fold, and I will warm myself beside the sheep till dawn.
There is plenty of dry hay in the fold; your bellies will be full.
May your bounty increase, master... Within two days Akcha will give milk; I will bring the very first bowl to the guardhouse with my own hands.
The village pasture is narrow; if you hand over one of the two sheep to the barracks for slaughter, I will unbar the gate.

Master... Do not ask me to slaughter Karaca, you would tear out my heart. But look, let me give you this forged copper bell and the boxwood ladle at my belt. And every week I will leave the first fresh curd cheese at your door—do not part me from my souls.
Yesterday we refused entry to nomads coming down from the mountain; did you cross paths with them on the trail?

I did, master... They had lit a fire at the edge of the pine grove, wailing that the village gatekeeper drove them off to starve. Yet they had no sheep; they were remnants of mountain looters! I am only after my honest bread—do not destroy me.
There are many brigands on the mountain; did anyone follow your tracks?
I walked along the rocky ridge to hide my trail until my soles split. No one is behind me, though the smoke of the highland still stings my nostrils.
Winter is near; what use is a shepherd to the village?

A sheep is pure blessing. From its wool stockings are knitted, from its milk cheese is set, and its dung revives the garden. Nor do I sit idle; I muck out the fold, set wolf traps, and sense a wolf's howl on the wind.

yanitlar.kabul: May your abundance grow, gatekeeper! We shall curl up in the most sheltered corner of the fold. Tomorrow I will offer the first milk I draw to the village children and to Yusuf.
yanitlar.rusvet: Take this, master—tuck this fine forged copper bell inside your tunic. And two days from now, the first fresh curd cheese shall come straight to your table. Just open the gate.
yanitlar.ret: The night frost is about to settle into the valley... If my beasts freeze, I cannot live on either. May the sin of these mute souls rest upon your neck.

not: Accept first. After one reply, Bribe and Reject unlock. No Barracks.
acilis: Two sheep and a cracked milk pail are all I have left in my hands. Mongol riders set the highland pasture ablaze; when I saw the smoke, I turned the rest of the flock loose onto the mountain and brought these two behind me. A corner of a sheepfold is enough for us.

sahne: A broad-shouldered master craftsman whose hands and face are blackened with iron soot. Bound to the rope on his back he carries a piece of leather bellows and a cracked hammer; he has no anvil, yet an unquenched forge fire burns in his eyes.
sorular: You say your anvil is gone and your bellows burned; when a smith abandons his hearth, did you receive leave from the Ahi guild elder, and where is your journeyman?

An anvil weighs five hundred okkas, gatekeeper! When fleeing for one's life, does a man carry his soul or a block of iron? Our bazaar was raided, my journeyman stayed in the citadel, and I took leave from the elder to keep the forge alive from village to village. Give me a bowl of charcoal and a fistful of scrap iron, and behold my skill!
When Mongol riders raided, you left your master behind and fled, did you not? Who trusts a runaway journeyman?

M-my master... He shouted, 'Save the bellows, lad, let the craft not die!' The roof of the shop was ablaze; had I tried to go back in, I would have been roasted alive! Yes, I fled... Every night in my dreams I see the flames of that hearth! If you doubt me, take this hammer and strike my head, but do not insult my craft!
Master Karaca is our village blacksmith; will you be able to stand before him and explain this?

Master Karaca? Is our Ahi father Master Karaca in this village? Ah... I was his apprentice once! I will kneel before him and pour out both my sin and my skill! Take me to his hearth, gatekeeper, and let him pass judgment upon me!
kacak_kalfa
Since you saved the lungs of the bellows, the craft is not dead. Is your wrist strong?

My wrist is harder than stone, master! The fire of the hearth has entered my blood. Give me rotten iron, and I will draw out a spearhead supple as a bow. With one pull of the bellows I bring iron to temper.
The village plowshares are blunted and the axes are dull; there is much work.
I will line them all up, master! From dawn prayer till nightfall I will make the anvil ring. Not a single sickle tooth in the village will remain dull.
What do you hide in that leather pouch at your sash? I caught a yellow gleam.

Nothing escapes your eye, master guard... It is half an okka of pure brass ingot I salvaged from my master's hearth. Hook it to your belt; melted down, it is worth ten silver pieces. Open my forge, and this ingot is yours.
We admitted the clothier from Kayseri; were you in the same caravan with him?

Master Selim the clothier? If you took him in, you have found the path of righteousness, master! It was I who forged the iron spindles of his loom! Let him weave the cloth and I will sharpen his shears; together we two shall liven up this village's market.
We have stone quarries in our village where axes snap and scythes dull. Are you truly a master of your trade?

Give me scrap iron and I will turn out a hoe hard as steel. I know the tempering of a blade as well as the shoeing of a horse. I received my license from the Ahi line and never struck hammer to unlawful iron.
Will you forge swords and shields for the barracks, or do you only mend plows?
When needed, I forge both armor and spearheads! I learned how to temper steel from the masters of Tokat Castle. I pour my sweat so the soldier's shield is unpierceable and his sword unbreakable.

yanitlar.ret: Do not do this, master guard... Do not waste the strength in my wrist against bare stone. If I am left outside, this hammer will rust in my hand, and I will have no face left to show Master Karaca.
yanitlar.kabul: May your hearth never know sorrow! Tomorrow morning when you hear the first ring of the hammer, you will say, 'It is well we opened the gate.' I will gladden Master Karaca's bellows.
yanitlar.kisla: Give me the barracks forge! I will melt down broken arrowheads and tighten the rivets on your shields. No soldier's weapon will wobble in his grip—I vouch for it.

not: Reject first. After one reply, Accept and Barracks unlock. No Bribe.
acilis: I am a blacksmith... My anvil is gone, and half my bellows burned in the fire, yet this wrist of mine still swings a sledge. Show me a hearth corner, and I will sharpen the sickles and swords of this village.

sahne: The iron helmet on his head is dented from a heavy blow, and the scabbard at his waist hangs empty. Beneath his torn mail he has grown gaunt enough for his ribs to show; on his face is both barracks shame and the hard gaze of a soldier who has returned from death.
sorular: You say you lost your sword in a brigand ambush in the Erzincan gorge; while the whole company scattered, where was your subashi, and how did brigands seize the pass?

Our company commander fell from his horse at the first spear, brother! They rolled boulders down from both slopes of the mountain; the horses panicked and the ranks split. I did not sell my weapon for bread—I saved my life by tumbling down the crags. I let no man slander my honor!
You lie! You did not sell it to an innkeeper; you surrendered your sword as tribute to the Karaboran brigands, did you not?

Enough, gatekeeper! Do not press me! Five horsemen surrounded me... 'Drop the sword and we spare your life,' they said! What honor remains to an unarmed soldier? I was starving and wounded... Yet I saved my life to bring warning to this border!
Confessing the truth is also valor. If you enter the barracks, do you have the strength to hold a spear?
My strength lies in my fury, master! Give me a spear; if those brigands come before this rampart, I will demand the reckoning of my sword from their lungs!
It is not for us to reproach a wounded and starving soldier... How many days have you been on the road?
For four days I have chewed dry grass, master... Nothing save fountain water has entered my throat. Give me a bowl of hot bulgur, and I will stand like a statue at the watchpost.
Hot tarhana soup boils on the barracks hearth; step inside.
May God be pleased with you, brother... May my spear snap in my hand if I forget this kindness.
Yesterday we admitted the trooper from Sivas into the barracks; do you know him?

The spearman from Sivas? I know him, master—he is the madman who drove his lance straight into an armored horse in the gorge! If he survived, your barracks stands firm as a fortress; put me beside him and let us keep watch back to back.
pusat_kaybi
Judging by your dented helmet, a heavy mace struck your head; are your wits intact?

A mace grazed me as it passed, master. For two days my ears rang and I saw the world double, but thank God it passed. My wits are sound; I can press my ear to the earth and tell the hoofbeats of approaching cavalry.
Do your ears hear keenly; can you pick out sounds in the night?
Even if my eyes fail, my ears see, master! I can sense the stir of a badger in the brush and the clink of a horseshoe against stone from half a mile off. Put me in the watchtower and test me.
If you enter the village barracks, what will you do with an empty scabbard?

There are plenty of spare spears in the barracks. I will hold a spear, dig trenches, and drive stakes at the foot of the wall. A soldier's duty is not swinging a sword alone; labor and sentry watch are the glory of the corps.

yanitlar.kisla: Bless the threshold of the barracks! Give me a spear, and I am a coward if I blink on night watch. I shall fill my empty scabbard with brigand blood.
yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, brother. A dry awning by the village fence is enough for me. I beg no food for nothing; I will dig trenches and clear the moat.
yanitlar.ret: What can I do on this mountain peak without sword or shield? Will you leave a soldier as prey for wolves and crows? May your mercy wither...

not: Barracks first. After one reply, Accept unlocks. After two replies, Reject unlocks. No Bribe.
acilis: Greetings, brother sentry... Our company was shattered in the Erzincan gorge. I lost my sword in a brigand ambush, yet these two eyes of mine suffice to keep watch at the gate, and my ears to listen to the plain.

sahne: On his back he carries a plow beam with a cracked iron share, and knotted at his sash is a small sack of barley seed. His muddy toes are numb with frostbite; in his eyes dwells a deep dignity tempered by grief for his children.
sorular: The plow is broken and there is no ox. What will you till the earth with in this winter storm, old plowman?

My ox went into a Mongol cauldron, master... Yet I can have the plowshare reforged at the smithy and harness myself to the beam! If the earth stays hungry, man stays hungry too; I know the language of the soil.
The barley seed at your sash reeks of mold! If you cast that seed into the field, you will poison the village crop as well!

It is not mold, master, I beg you do not say so! Only two ears caught dampness... Spread it in the sun and mix it with wood ash, and within a week it will be spotless! My two sons fell martyr saving this seed from the burning granary... Their blood is on this sack; do not make me throw it away!
We honor the memory of your sons, yet the village granary cannot be put at risk.
Do not put it in the granary, master! Give me the stony slope outside the fence and let me plant it grain by grain with my own hands! If it sprouts rotten, banish me from the village!
Your feet are frostbitten and your sash is soaked... Is this seed all that remains of your sons?

Only this seed and this cracked plowshare remain, master... Both are witnesses to twenty years of toil. Do not part me from the soil; a landless peasant is like a fish out of water—I will thrash and die.
We have Master Karaca in our village; he can reforge your plowshare in his hearth and revive it.
May Master Karaca's hands never know pain... Let him weld the share, and I will fill the village granary with barley.
Yesterday we admitted a farmer from Erzincan with his yellow seed; do you know him?

Halil of Erzincan? Did he escape the fire on the plain too? Ah, master, if his millet and my barley stand side by side, this village will never know winter famine! Put us both in the same field and let abundance gush forth!
You said your village was torched, plowman; did you not send word to the Ahi settlements on the plain, and did no one spot you on that narrow footpath as you fled?

Did they leave us breath to send word, gatekeeper... At midnight they plunged in like wolves and hurled torches onto the roofs. I overturned the cart and hid in the brush, lying in the mud until daybreak. No one saw me.
Will you share in the village granary, or look only after your own portion?
Without unity there is no peace, gatekeeper! My seed becomes the village's seed, and the village's bread becomes food for our table. He who eats alone finds only grief.
yikilmis_koy
Will you share in the village granary, or look only after your own portion?
Without unity there is no peace, gatekeeper! My seed becomes the village's seed, and the village's bread becomes food for our table. He who eats alone finds only grief.

yanitlar.rusvet: Master... Let me pour half of the fine seed barley at my sash into your private pouch. Two handfuls of barley are worth gold in winter. Let me pass.
yanitlar.ret: I cannot turn back onto the road, master; the soles of my feet are split open. I will curl up at the base of the stone and wait for dawn, though I know not if my life will hold out. May the sin of my children rest upon your neck.
yanitlar.kabul: May your soil brim with abundance! I will have Master Karaca weld this broken plowshare and raise double the barley for the village. May your hearth smoke forever.

not: Bribe first. After one reply, Reject unlocks. After two replies, Accept unlocks. No Barracks.
acilis: They set our village ablaze, master guard... As we fled, the ox-cart overturned and my plow struck a boulder and split. I left two children behind and could salvage only this handful of seed. Even with a broken plow, I have the strength to till the earth.

sahne: A cobbler journeyman whose eyes are bloodshot from sleeplessness. Skeins of waxed thread and a rustless leather awl hang from his sash; a faint metallic clink comes from the lining of the leather saddlebag on his back.
sorular: You say the bazaar burned to ash and you barely escaped the shop; where did the fire start in the great saddlers' market, and did the guild warden not guard the shops?

The warden barred the khan gate, but looters set fire to the wooden eaves from behind, master. Flames engulfed the arcade in an instant. In fear for my life I thrust my awl and needles into my sash and escaped. The shop burned, yet the skill in my hands did not.
A gleam of silver shows beneath the leather lining of your bag; what did you pilfer from the fire, apprentice?

I-I pilfered nothing, master! It was a silver belt buckle flung across the threshold as my master's mansion burned... Its owner turned to ash, and had it stayed on the ground it would have been crushed under a Mongol hoof! By God I am no thief—I tucked it into my breast to sell if I starved!
Will you surrender that buckle and pay penance through your craft?
I will surrender it, master! Take the buckle and place it in the village chest! Just give me a scrap of sole leather and beeswax so I may stitch the villagers' sandals and the guards' scabbards!
Your eyes are bloodshot and your fingers are pricked raw from stitching needles... Are you hungry?
For two days I have swallowed smoke, master... I forgot my hunger, though my fingers are numb with frost. If I find the warmth of a tandoor in a corner, I will mend all the torn shoes in the village.
We have a tanner and a felt-maker in our village; there will be work for you.
I stitch oak-acorn tanned hide so tightly that five winters may pass and not a drop of water will seep through!
We admitted the clothier from Kayseri who came yesterday; were you together in the bazaar fire?
The master draper? I saw him, master! As he clutched his bolt of cloth and ran, I watched him go and wished I had saved a roll of leather too. Let him cut the cloth, and I will stitch the lining!
kacak_sarac
Besides stitching rawhide sandals, what else are your hands suited for?
Not shoes alone, gatekeeper; I reinforce horse saddles, sew arrow quivers, and tie grain sacks with knots that never unravel. A stitcher is a man who patches every tear.
Are you willing to wait by the gatepost if the villagers do not take you in right away?
I am willing, master. I will crouch on a stone and stitch the first torn sandal placed before me. Let my work prove my skill, and I leave the rest to the villagers' conscience.

yanitlar.ret: Very well, master guard. I will sit upon the gate threshold and stitch whatever torn leather comes to hand till dawn. When day breaks, I will seek the villagers' goodwill through my craft.
yanitlar.kabul: May Khidr be your companion, gatekeeper! In this village no one's foot shall touch bare stone again; I will go over every boot and sandal and make them sound.
yanitlar.rusvet: Master guard... The sole of your boot has parted and the leather drinks water. Let me give you that silver buckle from my bag and sew a waxed double stitch onto your boot. I ask not a single coin—just unbar the gate.

not: Reject and Accept from the start (reject threshold 0 required). After one reply, Bribe unlocks. No Barracks.
acilis: When our bazaar turned to ash, I barely saved my life from the shop... I carry no hides on my back, yet at my sash I have my awl and cord, and in my hands the skill of stitching. Even at the gatepost I can mend the villagers' sandals and harness and earn my keep.

sahne: A sturdy bow of knotted maple hangs from his shoulder, yet not a single arrow remains in the leather quiver on his back. A horn thumb-ring gleams on his thumb; his gaze is as keen and vengeful as a hawk's.
sorular: You say you fought down to your last arrow in the mountain pass; what clan were those brigands you shot, and who held up the Turkmen convoy trailing behind on the mountain?

They were black-capped brigands, master... They had seized the pass and tried to rob the migration caravan. I brought three of them down from the crags; when their horses bolted, the convoy pulled back and took shelter in the woods. My arrows ran out, yet those innocents saved their lives.
You escaped alone; what became of the comrades you left behind?

Two of my comrades were shot in the back in the pass, gatekeeper... Not by an enemy arrow, but by the arrow of a treacherous sentry among us! I snapped their bows so they would not fall to the brigands! I am on the trail of that traitor; I came here both to hold the gate and to track that scoundrel!
No traitor shelters in our village! Is there someone at the gate you suspect?
I can scent a trail, master. He is not here yet, but I know he is drifting toward this border. Give me arrows and post me on the tower; I can tell friend from foe like a bird in flight!
The horn thumb-ring on your finger is master-crafted... You look weary, trooper.

I have drawn the bowstring since I was seven years old, master. Weariness passes, yet an empty quiver is a disgrace to a soldier. I hid my bowstring inside my tunic so the damp would not slacken it. Give me a handful of arrowheads, and I will let no mountain jackal near the village.
The wind blows fierce atop our tower; can you endure the watch?
The wind is my brother, master. I scent the wind and aim two fingers ahead of the mark. While my eye is on the plain, let the village folk sleep in peace.
Yesterday we admitted the wounded spearman who came to our gate; are you from the same banner?

The infantryman with the broken lance? Yes, master! While he fought in the trench at the Sivas pass, I was raining arrows from the ridge above! Praise be that he survived; put me beside him—let him hold the spear and I will draw the bow!
bos_sadak_kemankes
The village's stock of arrows is low; where shall we find arrows for you to spend?

I cut shafts from reed beds and bind fletching from hen feathers! A master archer makes his own arrows, master. Just give me iron arrowheads, and from the watchtower I will shoot a bird through the eye.
Will you obey the village warden and its discipline without condition?
My word is my bond, gatekeeper. Just as an arrow loosed from a drawn string never turns back, a bowman's word never turns back once spoken. My life is entrusted to this village's wall.
Will you obey the village warden and its discipline without condition?
My word is my bond, gatekeeper. Just as an arrow loosed from a drawn string never turns back, a bowman's word never turns back once spoken. My life is entrusted to this village's wall.

yanitlar.ret: To send me back unarmed into these crags is to hand me over to the executioner, gatekeeper... Though my quiver is empty, my heart was full; you have done a grievous wrong.
yanitlar.kabul: Bless you! I will climb straight to the watchtower. My eye will be on the plain, my hand on the bowstring. If a stranger approaches, the village folk will not hear of it before I do.

not: Reject first. After one reply, Accept unlocks. No Barracks and no Bribe.
acilis: I am a bowman of the frontier marches, gatekeeper... My bow stands sound, though my quiver is empty. In the mountain pass I fought down to my last arrow; I felled several and scattered the rest. Give me arrows, and I will guard your gate and towers with my life.

sahne: A young peasant clad in torn coarse felt. In one hand he holds a fired clay water jug, and in the other half a loaf of bread wrapped in clean linen; his eyes are gentle, sorrowful, and resigned.
sorular: You say your camp scattered from drought and raids; where did your clan bey withdraw, and where were the parents of those orphans you met on the road?

Our bey withdrew to the highland pasture with the remaining livestock, leaving the poor folk forsaken on the plain, master. Those orphans' tent burned before my very eyes; their mother and father perished in the flames. Not a morsel would have passed my throat had I not shared my bread with them.
You stoppered the jug with oak wood; does it hold smuggled wine or opium rather than water?

God forbid, master! Where would a poor peasant find opium! In this jug is the last sweet must of our camp's century-old vine stock... Before our camp dried up and scattered, my mother filled this jug and told me, 'If you reach a village with a smoking hearth, pour it upon their soil for blessing.' There is nothing unlawful inside!
Your mother's bequest is honored... Are you willing to pour it upon the village vineyard?
I am willing, master! Better still, if there is a master vintner here, let me give it to him to rub on the graft shoots so my camp's blessing may live on in this village's vineyard.
A man who shelters orphans has a place at our table. Did anyone else survive from your camp?

Some turned south toward the Aleppo road; others took refuge in the crags. I struck out north to seek a hearth where peace still smokes. Those two little children I met on the road prayed for me, and that prayer carried me all the way here.
In our village Sister Ayse and Saruca Hatun distribute food to orphans; you can help them.
I will haul firewood for Sister Ayse's cauldron and shoulder sacks for Saruca Hatun's granary! Only place me beneath an eave.
Did you see the refugees we turned away from the gate down on the plain?

I saw them, master... I offered them each a sip from my jug. They said the guard at the gate would not hear them out. I told them, 'Every gate has its hour, and every guard has his burden.' And I waited in patience.
fedakar_genc
The village garden lies on stony ground; will you swing a pickaxe and spade?
Spading a garden is my ancestral craft, master. I climb down wells to clear stones, channel water from the ditch, and swing the hoe. Whatever soil my hand touches turns green, by God's leave.
You are worn out from hunger; do you swear not to stretch your hand unlawfully toward the village granary?
What need is there for an oath, gatekeeper! May my mother's milk be unlawful to me if a single forbidden morsel enters my throat. I covet nothing beyond the food I earn.

yanitlar.ret: My neck is thinner than a hair, gatekeeper... Since the gate will not open, I will set my jug upon the ground at the threshold and wait for the dawn call to prayer. God is great.
yanitlar.rusvet: Master... I have no worldly wealth in my hands, yet let me pour this ice-cold spring grape must from my jug into your bowl to refresh your heart. Let us share the half loaf too—only do not leave me outside.
yanitlar.kabul: May your heart never know sorrow, master guard! I will go straight to the wellhead and draw the buckets. I pledge my life to this village's garden and its orphans.

not: Reject first. After one reply, Bribe unlocks. After two replies, Accept unlocks. No Barracks.
acilis: Our camp scattered from drought and raids, master... All that remains in my hands is the grape must in this jug and half a loaf of bread. I shared it with orphans I met on the road; this is what is left. Grant me shelter beneath an eave, and I will pour my sweat into your vineyard and garden.

sahne: A cracked wooden shield hangs from his shoulder, and his right arm is bound to his chest from elbow to wrist in a soiled sling. His boots are caked in mire up to the knee and his breath rattles in his chest; in his eyes mingle the bitterness of defeat and a soldier's pride.
sorular: You say you held the stone bridge for two days and nights; why did the castle garrison at the other end of the bridge send no aid, and how was the embankment breached?

The garrison was besieged, master; they had no troopers left to spare for the bridge. The cavalry found a shallow ford along the riverbed with their armored mounts and flanked us from behind. Our shields were splintered, yet we stood till our last breath.
While your sergeant fought on, you took fright and fled without looking back, did you not? A runaway soldier never runs out of excuses!

My sergeant sent me ahead shouting, 'Warn the villages, have them man the battlements!' gatekeeper! Would a coward crawl through mud for two days with a mangled arm? If you doubt me, take this cracked shield and smash it against my chest, but never call me a coward! Fifteen of my comrades fell into the earth at that embankment!
Your anger is just, trooper. Are you ready to report the situation to the warden in the barracks?
I am ready, master! I will spread the map before the warden and point out every culvert the horsemen can cross. Post me on the tower, and if anyone approaches I will sound the horn!
The blood on your arm is fresh and you shiver... Come, let us pour a bucket of water and cleanse your wound.

May God be pleased with you, brother... For three days I feared my arm would rot with gangrene. If I find a pinch of salt and a splash of vinegar, I can bind it myself. A soldier's life is entrusted to the realm.
We have a Roman healer named Miraen in our village; she will tend to your arm.
I have heard of Miraen Hatun's learning, master... Let her cleanse the wound, and by morning I will haul rampart stones even if only with my left hand.
Yesterday we admitted a bowman to the tower; he spoke of the ambush in the pass—did you see him?

The bowman from Tokat? I saw him, master! It was he who rained arrows down upon the brigands from the ridge, shouting that a traitor had shot from behind! If he is safe, our tower is secure; put me beside him and let us stand lookout together.
yarali_gazi
If you are admitted to the barracks, what use will you be with that wounded arm?

In the barracks I will climb the watchtower! Though my right arm is in a sling, with my left hand I can blow the horn and give tactics to the sentries on the wall. I know like the palm of my hand which part of the gorge is craggy and which gives passage to cavalry.
If cavalry approaches, how will you fight with a single arm?
My one arm holds a shield and my chest becomes a rampart, master! I will brace against the gate leaf and trip the horseman's mount. A true soldier never stands idle.
Did anyone else from the sanjak bey's company survive behind you?

Our sergeant was still swinging his sword by the ditch when last I saw him... He sent me ahead saying, 'Run to the ridge and carry word to the villages behind.' I fulfilled my duty and reached your gate.

yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, master guard. I will find clean water by the infirmary wall and wash my wound, apply Miraen Hatun's salve, and take my turn on watch when called.
yanitlar.ret: Will you drive me beyond the trench with this bleeding arm? By night the cavalry patrol sweeps the plain; you will find my lifeless body in the brush... May the sin be upon your neck.
yanitlar.kisla: Bring me straight before the castle warden! The embankment in the gorge has collapsed, and I must show the horsemen's route upon the map. Let one more life be pledged to the barracks.

not: Accept, Reject, and Barracks from the start.
acilis: My shield is cracked and my arm is in a sling, master guard... We held the stone bridge behind us for two days and two nights, yet the cavalry broke through the embankment. Even if I have no strength left for pitched battle, I have eyes to keep watch at your gate and breath to warn of approaching peril.

sahne: Forged copper bowls and ladles clatter against one another inside his donkey's saddlebags. His apron is smeared with hearth soot, and the gash above his left brow has not yet scabbed over; suspicious metallic weights can be felt at the bottom of his pack.
sorular: You say you fled along the creek when the marketplace was raided; with the copper bowls clattering in your saddlebags all down the valley, how did brigands not pursue you?

I stuffed dry grass and felt between the bowls, master! I even wrapped felt around the donkey's hooves so not a sound would escape. By night I mingled with the rushing sound of the creek and slipped past the crags. A craftsman knows how to be resourceful.
Why is the bottom of that large cauldron on your donkey's back double-riveted? Is there smuggled metal inside?

Hush, master, I beg you... Inside the double bottom I hid not smuggled ore, but pure mercury powder sought by alchemists and an ingot of refined tin! While the bazaar was being looted, I concealed them so they would not fall into brigand hands! If it comes to light, Master Karaca will drive me from his hearth! I will give you whatever you ask, only do not announce it to the folk!
If you donate that metal to Master Karaca's smithy, the gate will open.
Agreed, master, upon my head! Let Master Karaca use it for the smithy and apply mercury solder to the village shields! Only let me practice my craft in this village!
The cut on your brow is fresh and your eyes are full of dust... Do you have a morsel of food?

I had two pieces of dry biscuit in the donkey's feedbag, and I shared those with the beast, master. If you give me a bowl of hot soup, I will polish all the sooty pots in the village till they gleam like gold.
The village cauldrons await tinning before winter so they do not taint the food with verdigris.
I will light the hearth early tomorrow morning, master! Sal-ammoniac smoke will curl through the square, and all the copperware will shine like a mirror.
We admitted the cobbler journeyman who came yesterday; he has already begun stitching shoes.
That orphan apprentice from the bazaar? Ah, his stitching is sound, master! Let him sew the shoes and I will polish their brass buckles; let the village market come alive again!
supheli_bakirci
There is little copperware in our village; the folk use clay pots. What use is a tinsmith here?

Clay cracks and shatters, while copper lives a thousand years, gatekeeper! You must tin the village soup cauldron so it does not poison the broth. I also forge horseshoes and door hinges; my hand knows every metal.
What is that gash on your brow—were you in a brawl?
As I fled, the great cauldron atop the workbench toppled over, master. Trying to catch it, its rim split my brow. A copper edge cuts skin, yet love of the craft stands above life.
Are the bowls in your saddlebag lawful goods, or did you gather them from the looting?

I am a tinsmith registered in the Ahi line, master! Stamped on the bottom of every bowl is my own hammer mark. Not a single scale of metal I did not forge by the sweat of my brow has ever entered my bag.

yanitlar.rusvet: Look here, master... Let me leave you this fine cast yellow copper bowl so you may drink soup by the hearth, and let the mercury solder powder beside it be my gift as well. Do not let Master Karaca hear of it—keep it between us and draw back the bolt.
yanitlar.kabul: I will tie the donkey in a sheltered corner of the courtyard and toss two handfuls of hay before the beast, then curl up beneath the awning myself. First thing tomorrow I will polish the village cauldrons and pay my respects to Master Karaca.
yanitlar.ret: I cannot stay out in the open country alone with this load, gatekeeper! Looters who hear the clatter of copper will fall upon my throat. Was this the whole of your mercy?

not: Bribe, Accept, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a tinsmith of the lower districts, gatekeeper... My donkey carries the bowls, and I lead the donkey's halter. When the marketplace was raided, amidst naphtha and smoke I loaded my saddlebags and climbed up along the creek bed. Grant me a hearth corner so the cauldrons of this village do not go untinned.

sahne: In his arms he holds a frail goat kid whose broken left leg is splinted with wood. His felt vest is torn to shreds and his bare knees bleed from thorn scratches; he presses the kid to his chest like an infant.
sorular: You say you could not leave this lame kid when brigands raided the fold; while the flock scattered up the mountain, who was the chief of those brigands, and why did they not shoot you along the creek?

It was the band of the Red-Bearded brigand, master! They chased after the fattened rams in the fold and did not even glance at this poor lame kid. Taking the little one in my arms, I turned onto the goat path at the foot of the cliff.
It was not wolves that raided the fold, but the Red Crow brigands to whom you owed debt, was it not? You will draw their trail to this village!

Yes, I had a debt, master... Last winter when the fold collapsed I borrowed three coins from a usurer, and the brigands demanded ten sheep in interest! When I could not pay, they torched the fold! I scattered the flock onto the mountain so the debt could not be seized! What fault has this kid? The fault is mine—punish me as you will, only do not cast this innocent creature to the wolves!
If brigands are on your trail, we must put the village sentries on alert.
Alert them, master! I waded through the water along the creek bed so even their hounds cannot find my scent. Yet if brigands come, I will haul firewood to the barracks and hold a spear too!
Your knees bleed from bramble thorns and your felt vest is in tatters... The little one in your arms is shivering.

I rubbed thyme oil on the kid's leg and bound it with wood splints, master. If we find a palmful of warm milk and a wisp of dry straw, within two weeks it will stand on its feet and be a companion to Yusuf's goat Karabash.
Yusuf also lost his goat on the mountain like you; you will be glad to meet him.
I heard of Yusuf's name on the mountain... His mother's prayer watches over him. I will entrust this kid to Yusuf; let the two of them run across the village meadow.
Yesterday we admitted the highland shepherd with his ewes Akcha and Karaca into the fold; do you know him?
Highlander Dursun? Ah, master, his ewe Akcha has abundant milk! Let him milk the ewes and give two sips to this orphaned kid, and the kid will be on its feet within two days!
topal_oglak
The village fold is full; why should we make room for a stranger shepherd?

Though I am a stranger, I know the wolves and birds of the mountain, master. I know which herb holds healing and which spring is poisoned. I will tend your flock like my own child and let no harm come to a single hair.
What is that wooden splint tied to its leg—will the bone knit?
Its leg split while leaping down the crags. I tied two dry branches and rubbed thyme oil over it. In two weeks it will stand up and skip like a true goat, bringing blessing to this village's fold.
If the brigands follow the creek trail, will the village not be endangered?
I walked against the current of the water, master; my tracks vanished in the floodwater. Have no fear—I will cast no shadow upon the fortress of this village.

yanitlar.ret: I will curl up at the base of the stone and pull my torn felt vest over the kid. Without blinking an eye I will wait for dawn, though the frost is bitter... If its life gives out, may the sin rest upon your neck.
yanitlar.kabul: May God never bring sorrow to your hearth! I will sleep in a corner of the fold; let this mute creature grow up beside Yusuf, and let me take root in the soil of this village. I will be a burden to no one.

not: Reject and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the shepherd of the fold on the slope... Last night when brigands raided the fold, I turned the flock loose onto the mountain, yet I could not leave this lame kid behind. Carrying this little one in my arms, I crossed the crags. Just show us an eave and a handful of dry straw.

sahne: A heavy salt sack sewn of coarse linen swings from his hemp belt. His hands are cracked from frost and salt burn, and dried salty sweat gleams on his left temple; a faint smell of sulfur rises from the bottom of the sack.
sorular: You say the salt lake caravan was ambushed on the steppe; while the mules were driven over the cliff, where were the khan guards along that route, and how did you hide the salt at your sash?

The khan had been left far behind, master; they laid an ambush in the middle of the steppe and stampeded the mules over the ravine. I crouched in a rock crevice and buried this salt bag against my chest. Salt is life; a man left without salt on the mountain rots away.
Salt is white; what is this ash-colored, sulfur-smelling powder at the bottom of your sack? Do you carry gunpowder saltpeter?

Master... A merchant weighs every mineral. On the rocky slope of the salt lake we found a vein of saltpeter... The caravan master said we could sell it to castle wardens for good coin. I harbor no ill intent! Take this saltpeter and give it to the village barracks so they may pour fuses at the foot of the wall! The bread earned from salt is enough for me!
If you surrender the saltpeter to the barracks, no reckoning will be demanded of your caravan.

I surrender it gladly, master! Let the saltpeter go to the barracks, and let the pure rock salt enter your granary! This winter the villagers' meat will not spoil and their cheese will stay firm as stone.
Your hands are cracked from salt burn and the fissures are filled with blood... You must be in pain.

Salt burns a wound, yet it also kills the rot, master. My weariness comes from the weight of the salt. Give me a bowl of hot water to wash my cuts, and I will donate half the salt to the village granary.
Salt was nearly exhausted in our village granary; you arrived just in time.
Khidr sent me, master! All winter long I will cure the provisions of the granary so not a single piece of meat goes to waste.
Yesterday we admitted a tinsmith whose saddlebag held yellow copper bowls.

Master Mahmut the coppersmith? I know him, master—we drank soup together at the Kayseri khan! If he polishes the copper bowls, I will fill them with pure rock salt, and the village table shall be enriched!
tuz_kervani_kacak
Salt is scarce in our village granary; will you let us have it cheaply?

I am no profiteering merchant, master. Grant me a hayloft to shelter my head and a bowl of hot bulgur at dusk, and I will donate half the salt to your granary. With the rest I will barter fairly in the village.
Is the salt at your sash pure white, or muddy sediment from the lake?
It is pure mountain salt, crystal-white rock salt, master! It has never touched mud. A single pinch keeps a whole cauldron of meat from spoiling and holds cheese firm as stone.
Have the looters on the steppe turned this way?
They were busy plundering the silk bales and silver in the caravan, scattering the salt on the ground as dead weight. It will take them two days to reach here—make your preparations.

yanitlar.kabul: May you find abundance, gatekeeper! By the edge of the hayloft I will set the salt upon a dry plank and lie down beside it. All winter long I will not leave the meat and cheese of this village unsalted.
yanitlar.rusvet: Master guard... Let two handfuls of crystal salt and a pinch of saltpeter powder be poured into your pouch. In a frontier beylik it is more precious than silver. Add it to your soup and see your winter through; just let me inside.
yanitlar.ret: If I stand out in the open on this mountain peak, by night the jackals will catch my scent and come for the salt. I will hide behind the rocks and wait till dawn, yet if I lose my salt I am ruined.

not: Accept, Bribe, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a peddler who outfits caravans from the salt lake to carry goods to mountain villages, gatekeeper... Our caravan was ambushed on the steppe road and the mules were driven over a cliff. I could salvage only this fine rock salt at my sash. There is neither food nor realm without salt; open the gate so your village may prepare for winter.

sahne: A bent copper bugle hangs from the thick leather strap around his neck. His leather vest is split at the shoulder and the wooden scabbard of the sword at his waist is cracked; a fresh graze on his temple trickles blood down his cheek, and in his eyes lingers an averted look of kinship shame.
sorular: You say you lit the beacon before the tower was torched; how many times did you sound the horn before the tower fell, and did the sentry sergeant on the plain not catch your signal?

I blew three bitter blasts, master! The sound of the horn echoed across the valley. Yet they had raided the outpost on the plain at the same hour; when I saw the smoke, I knew it had fallen too. Had I not leaped from the cliff, I would have burned alive.
They say someone of your own blood was among those who raided the tower, and that is why you cut the horn blast short; is it true?

Who... Who told you that? Master... My uncle's son rode at the head of the brigand troop! 'Blow that horn and I will cut your breath!' he shouted! For a moment... For just a single moment I froze! Yet then I touched fire to the beacon and hurled myself over the cliff! I did not betray my post, master—blood ties clouded my mind for an instant, yet it was still I who came to warn your gate!
Even if he is your kinsman, if he approaches the border of this village he will be met with spears!
I know, master... Since he turned brigand, I have no kinsman left! I will blow my horn atop this village's tower so fiercely that even my cousin will tremble at my voice!
Your leather vest tore when you leaped from the cliff, and blood trickles from your temple... Catch your breath.

I tumbled down the cliff into the brush, master. Scratches matter little; the copper of my bugle is dented, yet its breath is sound. Give me a sip of water and let me climb the tower to stand lookout.
Our tower's bugle was broken; your arrival is a blessing.
Post me at the very top of the tower! I will spot cavalry dust from two miles off and rouse the village with a voice like the call to prayer.
Yesterday we admitted the wounded trooper into the infirmary; he told us the bridge embankment had collapsed.

The trooper from the stone bridge? Praise be that I see him alive! If he brought word of the embankment, I bring intelligence of fifty mounted raiders on the ridge; let the warden hear us both and take precautions!
borazanci_korkaklik_ithami
Your bugle was bent when you leaped from the cliff; does this copper still give voice?
Copper bends, yet its voice never bends, gatekeeper! The blast of this bugle will rouse the village from two miles away. Post me atop the rampart and let my eye watch the plain.
How many men raided the tower, and what color was their banner?
There were at least fifty horsemen, master! Wearing black fur caps, with wolf tails tied to the tips of their lances. They split into three columns and are sweeping down the valley.
Why should we not clap you in irons for taking fright and abandoning your post?

With the tower blazing like tinder, had I stayed inside I would have turned to ash, master! What use is a charred soldier to anyone? I saved my life to bring warning; even if you chain me, that is the truth.

yanitlar.kisla: Take me straight to the warden! I will describe step by step the dry creek bed the horsemen from the plain will follow, and hand my bugle to the lookouts on the tower so we do not lose this village to a raid.
yanitlar.ret: Will you leave me as an open target on this plain? Within two hours the horsemen will descend into the valley; you will find my corpse before your gate... May the sin rest upon your neck.
yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, brother. I will crouch at the foot of the infirmary wall and catch my breath, wipe the blood from my temple, gird my sword, and stand watch at the gate tonight.

not: Barracks, Reject, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the bugler of the hilltop watchtower, gatekeeper! The tower was raided; I lit the beacon torch, yet they rained arrows from the cliff. When the lower floor was set ablaze, I leaped from the precipice and tumbled into the valley. The dust of the horsemen behind me has not yet settled—open the gate so I may warn the warden!

sahne: In his arms he cradles a dry grapevine sapling whose roots are wrapped in damp burlap. The handle of the pruning knife at his sash is darkened with sweat; his palms are blistered and cracked, and the scent of fresh earth and sour grape must rises from the cloth around the sapling.
sorular: The village needs bread, vintner; where shall we find the patience to wait three years for grapes?

Does a grapevine yield grapes alone, master? From its leaves stuffed rolls are wrapped, from its unripe clusters sour verjuice is pressed, and from its raisins strength is found all winter long! A people who plant no vines perish in a single winter; a man who thinks of tomorrow plants a vineyard.
A sharp smell of sour must rises from the cloth wrapped around the graft shoot at your breast! Is this a Frankish wine-vine cutting forbidden by the zealots?

Master... A vineyard has both its lawful and its forbidden uses! This vine is a honey-muscat grape smuggled across the Byzantine border! A zealot may mistake it for wine, yet its dried raisins give strength to soldiers all winter and healing to the sick! If the village preacher objects, I will give its leaves to the soup kitchen and boil its molasses for the children! Do not snap the root, master!
If you share your knowledge with our village healer Miraen Hatun, permission will be granted to plant the vineyard.
Miraen Hatun knows the salve of the vine root as well, master! I will give her cuttings for medicine and grape leaves to Sister Ayse! Only let the sapling touch the soil!
Your palms are cracked, and you warmed the root against your chest so it would not dry out... A sip of our water is lawfully yours.

May God be pleased with you, master... I stinted my own throat to sprinkle water upon the root. If the root dies the vineyard dies, and if the vineyard dies hope dies. Give me the southern slope, and within two years the arbors will be painted green.
Our southern slope is stony, yet it catches plenty of sun; it will suit the vine.
The grapes of stony soil grow sweet, master! Gravel keeps the root warm and enriches its sugar. I will turn that slope into a paradise.
Yesterday we admitted a young peasant carrying grape must in his jug; are you kin to him?

The lad with the clay jug? I know him, master—he is an orphan from our upper valley! It was I who filled his jug with the last must of the camp! If that lad is safe, this sapling will not remain an orphan; we will pour his must upon the root of this sapling and awaken its abundance!
You say you were the vineyard watchman of the lower valley, whose grapes went to the beylik cellar; what did those who burned the vineyard do to the villagers, and why did they leave you alive?

They drove the villagers down to the valley floor, master, and torched the vineyard cottages. I hid inside the culvert of the aqueduct, and they took me for dead. When the fire died down to embers, I cut this lifeblood graft shoot from the soil and fled.
Did this sapling wrapped in cloth not freeze on the road?
At every spring I dampened its cloth and warmed it with the vapor of my own chest, master. The scent of ancestral soil still lingers on its root; the day you plant it, it will put forth shoots.
saraplik_bag_suphesi
Besides pruning vines, what use will you be to the village in winter?
In winter I weave baskets from pruned shoots, mend fences, and graft fruit trees. If a farmer's hand stops, his blessing flees; my hand never stops.

yanitlar.ret: I will crouch against the outer wall of the caravanserai and bury the sapling in damp mud. I can pass the night at the base of the stone, yet if the sapling withers my heart will burn...
yanitlar.kabul: May your soil rejoice, master guard! I will plant this sapling on the southern slope. Within three years the children of this village will come to your gate with armfuls of grapes, and I will offer its healing to Miraen Hatun.
yanitlar.rusvet: Look here, master... One is a honey-fig shoot and the other a seedless grapevine cutting. Plant them in your own garden and in two years you will harvest their fruit. Let these be yours, and bid me enter.

not: Reject, Accept, and Bribe from the start.
acilis: I am the vineyard watchman of the lower valley, gatekeeper... They set the vines ablaze, yet I dug up this fine graft shoot from the soil and tucked it into my breast. To one who waits three years in patience, this vine yields honey-sweet grapes. Grant me a slope and a span of earth so I may plant your vineyard.

sahne: An itinerant weigher whose brass dirhem weights clink at his sash and who carries a small hand balance in a leather pouch at his breast. The hem of his kaftan is torn and blood oozing from his heel is caked with mud; fine file marks glint upon the brass weights.
sorular: You say the market at the waystation khan was scattered; where is the caravan master of the khan, and did you not see the innkeeper or the sentries as you tucked your balance into your sash?

The innkeeper locked the doors, yet they smashed the gate with axes, master! To save the goods, the caravan master leaped onto his horse and rode into the woods. I wrapped my dirhem weights and balance into my sash and escaped up the kitchen chimney.
Hand me those dirhem weights! Why is the bottom of this five-dirhem brass block filed down? Did you do this to rob the villagers?

Master... When weighing at the judge's court a burr remained on the brass, so I filed it smooth! Not for fraud... That is, the merchants used coarse weights, and I wanted to protect my share! Very well... I confess: that five-dirhem piece is a quarter-grain short! When I could not pay the market extortion tax, I was forced to use that weight! Smash that weight, master! Take my scale if you must, only let me into the village so I may weigh with justice!
We have smashed the shaved weight! With the remaining sound weights you shall weigh the village market honestly!
Smash it, master, gladly! Let the crooked weight melt away and lift the sin from my neck! With my true weights I will not let a single grain of wheat in the village be weighed short!
hileli_dirhem
Your heel is torn open and blood is caked with mud... You can barely walk.

While running up the rocky footpath my leather sock split and a sharp stone pierced my heel bone, master. It burns with pain, yet the honor of a craft is greater than an aching foot. Two days of rest in a hayloft will suffice for me.
We have a salt merchant in our village; we will have salt water pressed to your wound.
A salt merchant? His rock salt will draw out the inflammation in my heel, master! It will sear the wound clean, and by morning I will take my place at the village scales.
Yesterday we admitted the rock-salt merchant; had you weighed his salt bales?

Ilyas the salt trader? Yes, master! Before the caravan was raided, he weighed his salt sacks upon my very balance! Let him bring the salt and I will set the dirhem weight, so the villagers may barter penny for penny!
How will you stand in the marketplace with that crippled foot?

My leather sock tore while running up the stony trail and my heel split open. If I rest two days in a corner of the hayloft, it will scab over. Even if the foot stays lame, the hand that holds the balance never trembles.
Are your remaining brass dirhems full weight, and do they bear the judge's stamp?
The other weights bear the sealed stamp of the sanjak judge, master! We cast the shaved one away; with the remaining weights, whatever is rightful comes out true.
Did the looters follow behind you?
They were slashing open the bales and scattering the wool, so they took no notice of me. I struck out up the goat path behind the stable toward the ridge. No one is following me.

yanitlar.rusvet: Brother guard... Here is a solid cast brass dirhem weight. Melt it down in the market and it fetches a tidy sum of coin. Hook it to your belt and let it be your due—only unbar the gate.
yanitlar.ret: With this mangled heel I cannot take a step across the open plain, gatekeeper... I will lean against the awning post and wait, yet if the breath of wolf and jackal touches the back of my neck tonight, I will not forgive my right.
yanitlar.kabul: May the scales of justice never waver! I will hold the balance in the village market and let no man cheat another of his due. A just market brings blessing to a village.

not: Bribe, Reject, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am a weigher who travels the highlands weighing wool and dyer's madder, gatekeeper... When the market at the waystation khan was broken up, I tucked my balance into my sash and bolted up the mountain. The scale weighs true, and when the hand holding it is honest, the market finds abundance. If you have a market, you have need of me.

sahne: On his back he carries a coarse mortar shovel with an iron blade. His fingertips are cracked and scabbed from lime burn; a fresh bruise from a falling stone stands out on his right shoulder, and his voice rumbles loud and fierce like a trench wind.
sorular: You say you grabbed your shovel and escaped through the culvert when the worksite was raided; is that huge bruise on your shoulder from a falling stone as you fled, or from the castle warden's cudgel?

As I fled, a cornerstone broke loose from the rampart face, master. I had laid that stone with my own hands; it turned out they had stinted the mortar, so the stone slipped and crushed my shoulder. Yet the warden's cudgel was no light matter either—we took plenty of threats because we saw those who stole from the mortar.
A wall does not collapse by itself! You saw the castle warden stealing lime and dressed stone from the mortar, and they beat you to silence you, did they not?

How did you know, gatekeeper? Yes! The warden had the lime hauled to his own vineyard and stuffed rotten rubble into the base of the rampart! Because I said, 'This wall will cave in at the first trebuchet stone,' they brought a timber beam down across my back and threw me into the moat! I crawled out through the water culvert of that moat! This village's palisade is made of wood too; he who knows not mortar is left without a fortress in two days!
A laborer who speaks the truth is welcome among us. Can you lay a stone foundation beneath our village's wooden palisade?

Stone foundations are my trade, master! I will pour such lime mortar around the base of the stakes that even if a Mongol battering ram strikes, the timber will not budge! Just provide me stone and lime!
rusvetci_dizdar_tanigi
Your fingertips are cracked from lime burn and dripping blood... Does it not hurt?

If a laborer's hand does not touch lime, it never grows calloused, master! It burns, yet I feel it no longer. Give me a bucket of water to wash off the lime; I am content with dry bread and a trench to shelter my head.
We have lime pits in our village; you can take up your work.
I will clean out the lime pits with my own hands! I will slake the quicklime with water and boil it so the rampart mortar sets hard as rock.
Yesterday we admitted a bowman to the tower; he complained of the weakness of the parapets.

The bowman on the tower spoke true, master! The base beneath the crenel is hollow; if two horsemen pull at it, the parapet will give way. Let him shoot the arrows, and I will lay stone beneath the parapet! Together we two will hold the wall like steel.
Our village wall is built of wooden stakes; what work is there for a stonemason here?

Wooden stakes are at the mercy of fire, gatekeeper! Who will lay the stone footing and lime fill around the base of the stakes? If you do not build the gate threshold of stone, cavalry horses will smash right through. Give me a shovel, and I will ring the village with trenches.
Can you swing a shovel with hands burned raw by lime?

If a laborer's hand never sees lime, it never forms calluses, master! It stings, yet I pay it no mind. I will knead mud with mortar and fortify the weakest stretch of the moat like a fortress in two days.
Will you join the barracks and dig trenches?
Digging the barracks moat is my bounden duty. A trench-digger knows well which soil caves in and where to dig a wolf-pit. It is the breastwork that saves a soldier's life.

yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, gatekeeper. I will sit on a stone and hold my shovel across my knees. Let me find a bowl of water to wash off the lime, and at first light I will be at the foot of the wall.
yanitlar.kisla: Send me straight to the barracks! I will show you which side of the trench is loose, reset the collapsed stones, and dig breastworks for the guards.
yanitlar.ret: I will climb down into the dry bottom of the ditch before the gate and lean on my shovel. If a wolf comes by night I will meet it with the iron blade, yet if this village's rampart collapses you will remember me.

not: Accept, Barracks, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a laborer who hauls stone and mixes mortar in the castle moat, gatekeeper... The worksite was raided; when horsemen lined the edge of the ditch, I grabbed my shovel and ran up through the culvert. My hands are split from lime, yet my body is hard as stone; I have come to build up your rampart and granary.

sahne: A hornbeam rolling pin hangs from his neck by a cord, and on his back he carries a dough trough carved from thick ash wood. His flour-dusted tunic clings to his chest with sweat, and a deep friction scrape marks his elbow; the sweet, tangy scent of sourdough starter wafts from his trough.
sorular: You say when horsemen burst into the bakery you leaped out the flour chute with your dough trough; how did you fit a huge trough through that narrow chimney, and what became of the flour sacks behind you?

It is a hornbeam trough left by my father, master—narrow in width and long in body. We had built the chute wide so flour dust would not clog it. The looters ripped open the sacks and the flour mingled with smoke; I pulled the trough through and jumped from the roof into the hayloft.
The flour residue at the bottom of your trough has turned black; is that poisonous ergot of rye? Do not poison the villagers!

I beg you do not say so, master! That is no poisoned rye—it is buckwheat sourdough starter roasted with black cumin! It is the forty-year-old sour starter of our hearth! Mix this starter into a bushel of flour, and by morning the rising dough will fill the whole village square with the fragrance of bread! Whoever eats of it on an empty stomach will feel his lungs rejoice!
The scent of bread is the morale of the villagers. Can you relight the village bakery oven?
I will light it, master! From the river stones of the village I will build a glowing tandoor, and for the soldiers I will bake campaign hardtack that keeps for three months without spoiling!
zehirli_un_suphesi
Your elbow is scraped raw and your floury tunic clings to your back with sweat... You are worn out.

I scraped it against the wall while jumping from the roof into the hay, master; so long as a baker's soul stays with his dough trough, he feels no pain. Give me a bowl of hot broth, and by morning I will pull the first loaf from the oven and bring it to your gate.
In our village the flour granary is under the stewardship of Saruca Hatun.
I know the blessing of Saruca Hatun! I will take her flour into my trough and spread abundance through the village without wasting a single flake of bran.
Yesterday we admitted a farmer with a broken plow who had saved his barley seed.

Uncle Idris the barley-grower? Ah, master, let us grind his barley at the mill, and from the barley flour I will bake winter loaves for the villagers! Together we two will never let the village go hungry!
The village flour is scarce and winter is near. Will a baker not drain the granary dry?

A master baker does not waste flour—he draws abundance out of flour, gatekeeper! Without sifting away the bran I knead whole wheat, and I bake soldiers' hardtack so well that it does not go stale for three months. From a single handful of flour I feed ten souls.
Did you get that bloody scrape on your elbow while falling down the chute?
I grazed the wall while leaping from the roof into the stable hayloft, master. The bone is sound. So long as a baker's hand kneads dough, an aching elbow is forgotten once two loaves are baked.
Do you have bricks to build an oven?
I will build a tandoor from the river stones of the village and plaster it with clay. Within two days the tandoor will glow red-hot, and the village folk will see the face of warm bread.

yanitlar.ret: I will hold the trough over my head as a shield and curl up beneath the awning. The frost will scatter my flour, yet I will guard my life. When the gate opens in the morning, I will seek my fortune again...
yanitlar.rusvet: Master... I have two pieces of fine dry biscuit baked with fragrant black cumin that I saved from the oven. Crumble them into your soup for flavor. Put them in your pouch and draw back the bolt.
yanitlar.kabul: May your hearth never know sorrow! By the edge of the hayloft I will set the trough beneath me and rest. Tomorrow morning give me the first flour from Saruca Hatun's granary, and I will set the tandoor smoking.

not: Reject, Bribe, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the baker of the waystation khan, gatekeeper... When horsemen burst into the bakery and looted the pantry, I shouldered my dough trough and leaped out through the flour chute. My trough is on my back, my rolling pin around my neck... Give me a bushel of flour, and by morning I will fill the village square with the warm scent of fresh bread.

sahne: Long farrier's pincers and a pair of iron horseshoes hang from his leather belt. His tunic is soaked in forge soot and sweat; his left heel is bound with a torn, soiled cloth stained with mud and clotted blood, and a notched brand upon the horseshoes gleams ominously.
sorular: You say the stallion snapped its chain and a horseshoe nail pierced your heel; how did a man with a nail in his foot crawl through that moat culvert, and why did the brigands not shoot you?

I clenched my teeth and yanked the nail out with my pincers, master! Then pressed mud and horse dung over it to staunch the blood. The brigands chased after the stallion, and no one looked twice at a limping farrier's apprentice. Crawling over the crags, I reached your gate.
That pair of horseshoes at your belt bears the three-notched brand of the Red Crow brigands! Are you the smith who shoes the outlaws' horses?

Master... They pressed a sword to my throat! In the Karaboran pass they cut off the caravan and told me, 'Either trim and shoe our horses' hooves or we throw you down the well!' Yes, I shod them... In fear for my life I shod them! Yet into the hoof of the last stallion I purposely drove the nail crooked so the mount would stumble! When that stallion reared up, the nail flew into my own heel! I am no traitor, master—I lamed the outlaw chief's horse and escaped!
If you lamed the outlaw's mount, the warden of the barracks will want to hear you.
